core: Distinctions among harmony, melody, rhythm, tempo, and texture
Chords, arpeggios, and chord progressions in an introductory Western framework
Context-sensitive use of consonance and dissonance
supporting: Triads as a three-note chord type
Basic listening for harmonic stability and change
Careful limits on universal emotional or cultural claims
outOfScope: Detailed chord spelling, Roman-numeral, key, or cadence analysis
Claims that every musical tradition uses harmony in the same way
Claims that consonance and dissonance have universal emotional meanings

claims.claim: Harmony concerns the simultaneous, vertical combination of pitches, which distinguishes it from a melody's successive pitch line.
In the cited introductory Western-music text, a chord is a group of three or more pitches sounding together and a triad is a three-pitch chord built with stacked thirds.
A series of changing chords is a chord progression, and a chord whose pitches are played separately is described as a broken chord or arpeggio in the cited text.

The cited text associates consonance and dissonance with relative stability and tension in its Western framework, while explicitly noting that perceptions are shaped by musical socialization as well as sound properties.
Texture concerns layers of sounds, melodies, and rhythms, so it should be distinguished from harmony even when a melody is accompanied by chords.
A listener can identify a harmonic change when simultaneous pitch combinations change even if a melody repeats, but should avoid naming exact chord labels when an excerpt does not support them.
